title: My cyberpunk pixel-art side-scroller
author: Yigidus
selftext:
I'm a pixel artist: I've been making pixel art for games for the last 5-6 years, and before that I was a 2D artist. This is the cyberpunk game and world I've had in my head since high school, and two weeks ago I finally started building it. It's still very early and there's a lot more polish to come, so I'd love your feedback.

How the art is made:

\- AI-assisted generation (PixelLab for characters / animation, GPT image kits for facades and signs)

\- everything mapped onto one 76-colour master palette

\- the characters and the world are my own designs; every generated asset gets reworked by hand in Aseprite

comments.author: glimsky
comments.body: Congratulations, I loved the result! I've always wanted to make a pixel art game but my artistic ability is poor. I could do very light retouching but the AI would have to do the heavy lifting. How viable do you think it is for non-artists to use the current tooling for pixel art games?

replies.author: Yigidus
replies.body: thanks! honestly it's more doable than ever. the tools get you pretty far now, the hard part is keeping everything consistent. my tip: pick one palette and one size for everything and stick to it, that alone fixes a lot. also i'm going pretty big and detailed with this one, which makes it way harder. if you don't have an art background i'd go with a simpler, smaller style, it's much easier to fix by hand. go for it

replies.author: glimsky
replies.body: I think your results are showing what I think will be the case with AI-assisted workflows for a while. The narrative is that everybody will lose their jobs. This \*may\* be the case, but I think that the most likely outcome will be that experts like you will be able to get amazing results (again, I really like your graphics) and people like me would get passable results. I could go without an artist if my gameplay is excellent, but you'd certainly have an advantage in the art department - which in gaming is a huge advantage.

replies.body: haha no, didn't give up on it, pixel art is still my main thing. for this project i use ai to get a base down fast, then the real work starts: everything gets mapped onto one palette, i clean up shapes and lighting by hand in aseprite, and the animations get fixed frame by frame (legs especially lol). the characters, the world and the story are all my own designs, i've been carrying this idea around since high school. as a solo dev it's the only way i could build something this big.basically i wanna try making something with the scope of cyberpunk 2077, but in pixel art.

replies.author: Yigidus
replies.body: I design and draw the characters and NPCs myself, then use PixelLab to get the animations and fix them frame by frame in Aseprite. Mobs take the longest since they have way more animations. ChatGPT is only for concepts and reference, never in the game. For environments and props I use Claude Opus 5.5 with Unity: Claude makes the rough version and I add the details on top. Good luck with yours!

replies.author: Yigidus

But honestly, without AI I wouldn’t have gotten even a quarter this far with the game.

comments.author: ItsDumi
comments.body:
Idk if you familiar with your code or nah but how does the dynamic lighting work? Are there regions/triggers on any given level that are essentially tinting the player as the pass through them? Or is it actually a light in some way? 

Looks greate, that's why I asked. It's not quite at the level of say, Replaced, but still really great and their lighting totally blew my mind.

replies.author: Yigidus
replies.body:
Real lights, no tint zones. It’s Unity’s 2D URP lighting: point/spot lights placed around the level (lamps, signs, windows), and the buildings have normal maps so the light actually wraps around the bricks and ledges. The neon signs are separate glow layers drawn additively on top, so they read bright even in dark areas. Paul just walks through the light pools like anything else.

I’m still working on the lighting though, it needs a lot more fine-tuning. And yeah, Replaced is the bar for me too, their lighting is unreal. Taking that as a compliment, thanks!

replies.author: ItsDumi
replies.body:
Thanks man! Very interesting stuff, i appreciate the detailed breakdown. If you want some advice (I was a cinematographer a few years back), I think you could play with depth more. I see foreground (the small bush in the indoor scene) but your shy xD go hard with the foreground! I love that first cut where you see the city in the distance. More Y-depth like that indoors with fg or even windows and those city layers again beyond them. Replaced had an insane amount of Y-depth and they could even move the player through it (which might be out of your scope and isnt totally needed). 

some silhouette of people smoking in the foreground, sitting with vr goggles or doing interesting, cyberpunky stuff yknow. Bring it to life a tad more.

Keep cooking 🔥

comments.author: RageshAntony
comments.body: how does the tilemap of the world work? procedurally generated or hand aligned ?

replies.author: Yigidus
replies.body: Hand-designed, nothing procedural at runtime. It’s not really a tilemap either: the streets are built from modular pieces (facades, shop fronts, props), and I wrote some editor tools that place them from a layout so I can iterate fast. After that I go in and adjust things by hand in the scene.
